claim: Susd4 gene codes for a transmembrane protein with four extracellular CCP domains.
source: The mammalian SUSD4 gene codes for a transmembrane protein with four extracellular CCP domains (Figure 1A) and is highly expressed in the central nervous system (Holmquist et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Holmquist et al., 2013.

claim: SUSD4 is highly expressed in the central nervous system.
source: The mammalian SUSD4 gene codes for a transmembrane protein with four extracellular CCP domains (Figure 1A) and is highly expressed in the central nervous system (Holmquist et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Holmquist et al., 2013.

claim: The SUSD4 gene is located in a genomic region deleted in patients with the 1q41q42 syndrome.
source: The SUSD4 gene is located in a genomic region deleted in patients with the 1q41q42 syndrome that includes developmental delays and intellectual deficiency (ID; Rosenfeld et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rosenfeld et al., 2011.

claim: The 1q41q42 syndrome includes developmental delays and intellectual deficiency.
source: The SUSD4 gene is located in a genomic region deleted in patients with the 1q41q42 syndrome that includes developmental delays and intellectual deficiency (ID; Rosenfeld et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rosenfeld et al., 2011.

claim: SUSD4 is among the 124 genes enriched in de novo missense mutations in a large cohort of individuals with autism spectrum disorders or intellectual disabilities.
source: SUSD4 is also among the 124 genes enriched in de novo missense mutations in a large cohort of individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) or IDs (Coe et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Coe et al., 2019.

claim: A copy number variation and several de novo mutations with a high CADD score have been described in the SUSD4 gene in patients with ASDs.
source: A copy number variation and several de novo mutations with a high CADD score, which indicates the deleteriousness of the mutations, have been described in the SUSD4 gene in patients with ASDs (Cuscó et al., 2009; denovo-db, Seattle, WA [denovo-db.gs.washington.edu] 10, 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Cuscó et al., 2009 and denovo-db.

claim: The SUSD4 protein regulates complement system activation in erythrocytes by binding the C1Q globular domain.
source: The SUSD4 protein has been described to regulate complement system activation in erythrocytes by binding the C1Q globular domain (Holmquist et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Holmquist et al., 2013.

claim: The C1Q globular domain is found in major synaptic regulators such as C1QA, CBLNs, and C1Q-like proteins.
source: Interestingly, this domain is found in major synaptic regulators such as C1QA (Stevens et al., 2007), CBLNs (Matsuda et al., 2010; Uemura et al., 2010), and C1Q-like proteins (Bolliger et al., 2011; Kakegawa et al., 2015; Sigoillot et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Susd4 mRNA expression increases during postnatal development in the cerebellum and brainstem.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR shows an increase in Susd4 mRNA expression (relative to the housekeeping gene Rpl13a) during postnatal development in the cerebellum and in the brainstem.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the cerebellum, Susd4 mRNA levels start increasing at P7 and by P21 reach about 15 times the levels detected at birth.
source: In the cerebellum, a structure where the developmental sequence leading to circuit formation and maturation is well described (Sotelo, 2004), quantitative RT-PCR showed that Susd4 mRNA levels start increasing at P7 and by P21 reach about 15 times the levels detected at birth (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HA-tagged SUSD4 is found in dendrites and in some of the distal dendritic spines in adult cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Immunofluorescent labeling against the HA tag demonstrated the localization of HA-SUSD4 in dendrites and in some of the numerous dendritic spines present on the surface of distal dendrites (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HA-tagged SUSD4 can be immunolabeled in non-permeabilizing conditions and located at the surface of dendrites and spines.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of transduced cultured PCs showed that HA-tagged SUSD4 could be immunolabeled in non-permeabilizing conditions and located at the surface of dendrites and spines (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Susd4 KO mice show impaired motor coordination adaptation and learning.
source: Motor coordination and learning is deficient in adult male Susd4 -/- (knockout [KO]) mice compared to age-matched Susd4+/+ (wild-type [WT]) littermates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by rotarod data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Susd4 KO mice performed as well as WT littermate controls on the first trial of the rotarod test.
source: The Susd4 KO mice performed as well as the Susd4+/+ (wild-type [WT]) littermate controls on the first trial (Figure 1F, day 1, trial 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by rotarod data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Control mice improved their performance on the rotarod as early as the third trial on the first day, while Susd4 KO mice showed no learning.
source: However, while the control mice improved their performance as early as the third trial on the first day, and further improved with several days of training, no learning could be observed for the Susd4 KO mice either during the first day, or in the following days (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by rotarod data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Susd4 loss-of-function leads to impaired motor coordination and learning in adult mice.
source: These results show that Susd4 loss-of-function leads to impaired motor coordination and learning in adult mice.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from the rotarod data.

claim: No deficits in the global cytoarchitecture of the cerebellum and morphology of PCs were found in Susd4 KO mice.
source: No deficits in the global cytoarchitecture of the cerebellum and morphology of PCs were found in Susd4 KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The firing properties of PCs are not affected by Susd4 loss-of-function.
source: No differences were detected in either the mean spiking frequency, the coefficient of variation (CV) of interspike intervals (ISIs), or the intrinsic variability of spike trains (CV2, Holt and Douglas, 1996), indicating that the firing properties of PCs are not affected by Susd4 loss-of-function.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on MEA recording data.

claim: There are no significant changes in the mean density and volume of VGLUT1 clusters following Susd4 loss-of-function.
source: High-resolution microscopy and quantitative analysis confirmed that there are no significant changes in the mean density and volume of VGLUT1 clusters following Susd4 loss-of-function (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No difference was observed in the amplitude and the kinetics of the responses to PF stimulation in PCs from Susd4 KO and control littermate mice.
source: No difference was observed in the amplitude and the kinetics of the responses to PF stimulation in PCs from Susd4 KO and control littermate mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The probability of vesicular release in the presynaptic PF boutons was not changed at PF/PC synapses in Susd4 KO mice.
source: Furthermore, the probability of vesicular release in the presynaptic PF boutons, as assessed by measurements of paired-pulse facilitation (Atluri and Regehr, 1996; Konnerth et al., 1990; Valera et al., 2012), was not changed at PF/PC synapses (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by paired-pulse facilitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No differences in the frequency and amplitude of PF/PC-evoked quantal events were detected in Susd4 KO mice.
source: Finally, no differences in the frequency and amplitude of PF/PC-evoked quantal events were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Susd4 invalidation has no major effect on the number and basal transmission of PF/PC synapses in the mouse.
source: Thus, in accordance with the morphological analysis, Susd4 invalidation has no major effect on the number and basal transmission of PF/PC synapses in the mouse.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from morphological and electrophysiological data.

claim: LTD induction and maintenance are greatly impaired in the absence of SUSD4.
source: In Susd4 KO PCs, the same LTD induction protocol did not induce any significant change in PF EPSCs during the 30 min recording period, showing that LTD induction and maintenance are greatly impaired in the absence of SUSD4 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by LTD data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The absence of Susd4 expression promoted LTP induction at PF/PC synapses.
source: In the case of Susd4 KO PCs, the same protocol induced LTP with a 27% increase in transmission that was maintained after 35 min (Figure 2E). These results indicate that the absence of Susd4 expression promoted LTP induction at PF/PC synapses.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by LTP data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CFs had a normal morphology and translocated along the proximal dendrites of their PC target in Susd4 KO mice.
source: We found that CFs had a normal morphology and translocated along the proximal dendrites of their PC target in Susd4 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference was found in the percentage of remaining multiply-innervated PCs in the absence of Susd4.
source: No difference was found in the percentage of remaining multiply-innervated PCs in the absence of Susd4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number and density of VGLUT2 clusters were not significantly different between Susd4 WT and Susd4 KO mice.
source: Furthermore, the number and density of VGLUT2 clusters were not significantly different between Susd4 WT and Susd4 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on quantitative analysis of VGLUT2 immunostaining.

claim: The typical all-or-none CF-evoked EPSC was detected in PCs from Susd4 KO mice with increased amplitude when compared to WT PCs.
source: Contrary to what could have been expected, the typical all-or-none CF-evoked EPSC was detected in PCs from Susd4 KO mice with increased amplitude when compared to WT PCs (Figure 3B) while no differences in CF-EPSC kinetics were found (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lack of CF-dependent PF/PC synapse LTD in Susd4 KO mice is not due to impaired CF/PC synapse formation or transmission.
source: Therefore, the lack of CF-dependent PF/PC synapse LTD in Susd4 KO mice is not due to impaired CF/PC synapse formation or transmission.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from CF/PC synapse analysis.

claim: Measurements of evoked quantal events revealed an increase in the amplitude of the quantal EPSCs at CF/PC synapses from juvenile mice.
source: Measurements of evoked quantal events revealed an increase in the amplitude of the quantal EPSCs at CF/PC synapses from juvenile mice (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The changes in PF/PC synaptic plasticity and in CF/PC transmission in Susd4 KO PCs have a postsynaptic origin.
source: Paired-pulse facilitation and depression at PF/PC and CF/PC synapses, respectively, are similar between Susd4 KO and control mice, both in basal conditions and during plasticity recordings (Figure 2C, Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting strongly that the changes in PF/PC synaptic plasticity and in CF/PC transmission in Susd4 KO PCs have a postsynaptic origin.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is an inference based on paired-pulse data.

claim: Susd4 loss-of-function in mice leads to a highly specific phenotype characterized by misregulation of postsynaptic plasticity in the absence of defects in synaptogenesis and in basal transmission in cerebellar PCs.
source: Overall our results show that Susd4 loss-of-function in mice leads to a highly specific phenotype characterized by misregulation of postsynaptic plasticity in the absence of defects in synaptogenesis and in basal transmission in cerebellar PCs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: The proportion of CF presynaptic boutons with no GluA2 cluster was smaller in juvenile Susd4 KO mice than in WT mice.
source: However, the proportion of CF presynaptic boutons with no GluA2 cluster was smaller in juvenile Susd4 KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The decrease in the proportion of CF presynaptic boutons with no GluA2 cluster partially explains the increase in the amplitude of quantal EPSCs and CF transmission.
source: This decrease partially explains the increase in the amplitude of quantal EPSCs and CF transmission (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is an inference based on GluA2 cluster analysis.

claim: After cLTD, a 35% mean reduction of surface GluA2 receptors was measured in slices from WT mice.
source: As expected, after cLTD a 35% mean reduction of surface GluA2 receptors was measured in slices from WT mice (Figure 4B; p=0.0212, two-tailed Student's t test with a null hypothesis of 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by surface biotinylation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In acute slices from Susd4 KO mice, a similar, but not statistically significant, mean reduction of surface GluA2 receptors was detected after cLTD.
source: In acute slices from Susd4 KO mice, a similar, but not statistically significant, mean reduction of surface GluA2 receptors was detected after cLTD (28%; p=0.0538, two-tailed Student's t test with a null hypothesis of 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on surface biotinylation data.

claim: SUSD4 loss-of-function does not lead on average to a major change in the activity-dependent regulation of the number of surface GluA2 subunits.
source: Thus, SUSD4 loss-of-function does not lead on average to a major change in the activity-dependent regulation of the number of surface GluA2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from surface biotinylation data.

claim: In slices from WT mice, chemical induction of LTD induced a significant reduction of 13% in total GluA2 protein levels.
source: In slices from WT mice, chemical induction of LTD induced a significant reduction of 13% in total GluA2 protein levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduction in total GluA2 protein levels after cLTD was prevented by incubation with the mixture of degradation inhibitors, MG132 and leupeptin.
source: This reduction was prevented by incubation with the mixture of degradation inhibitors, MG132 and leupeptin, showing that it corresponds to the pool of GluA2 degraded in an activity-dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In slices from Susd4 KO mice, activity-dependent degradation of GluA2 was completely absent.
source: In slices from Susd4 KO mice, this activity-dependent degradation of GluA2 was completely absent.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on western blot data.

claim: The chemical induction of LTD had no effect on the total protein levels of GluD2 in slices from WT or from Susd4 KO mice.
source: Additionally, the chemical induction of LTD had no effect on the total protein levels of GluD2, another synaptic receptor highly present at PF/PC postsynaptic densities, either in slices from WT or from Susd4 KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SUSD4 specifically controls the activity-dependent degradation of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors during LTD.
source: Thus, SUSD4 specifically controls the activity-dependent degradation of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors during LTD.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from GluA2 degradation data.

claim: HA-SUSD4 was detected in affinity-purified extracts after co-immunoprecipitation with SEP-GluA2, showing the specific interaction of SEP-GluA2 and HA-SUSD4 in transfected HEK293 cells.
source: After affinity purification of SEP-GluA2, HA-SUSD4 was detected in affinity-purified extracts while PVRL3α was not, showing the specific interaction of SEP-GluA2 and HA-SUSD4 in transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Clusters of HA-tagged SUSD4 partially colocalize with GluA2 clusters at the surface of some dendritic spines.
source: Clusters of HA-tagged SUSD4 partially colocalize with GluA2 clusters at the surface of some dendritic spines (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SUSD4 could regulate activity-dependent degradation of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors through a direct interaction.
source: Thus, SUSD4 could regulate activity-dependent degradation of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors through a direct interaction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a speculation based on interaction and colocalization data.

claim: Twenty-eight candidates were identified as potential SUSD4 interacting partners by proteomic analysis.
source: Twenty-eight candidates were identified including proteins with known function in the regulation of AMPA receptor turnover (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: Several candidates were functionally linked to ubiquitin ligase activity by gene ontology term analysis.
source: Several candidates were functionally linked to ubiquitin ligase activity by gene ontology (GO) term analysis (Figure 5A and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Five members of the NEDD4 subfamily of HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases were found as potential interacting partners of SUSD4.
source: In particular, five members of the NEDD4 subfamily of HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases were found as potential interacting partners, three of them (Nedd4l, Wwp1, and Itch) exhibiting the highest enrichment factors among the 28 candidates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on proteomic data.

claim: Immunoblot analysis of affinity-purified synaptosome extracts confirmed the interaction of SUSD4 with NEDD4, ITCH, and WWP1.
source: Immunoblot analysis of affinity-purified synaptosome extracts confirmed the interaction of SUSD4 with NEDD4, ITCH, and WWP1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Removal of the intracellular domain of SUSD4 prevented the interaction with NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Removal of the intracellular domain of SUSD4 (SUSD4ΔCT mutant) prevented this interaction demonstrating the specificity of SUSD4 binding to NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lack of the cytoplasmic domain completely abrogated binding of NEDD4 to SUSD4.
source: Lack of the cytoplasmic domain completely abrogated binding of NEDD4 to SUSD4, confirming the results obtained using synaptosome extracts (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminus domain of SUSD4 did not affect NEDD4 binding.
source: Deletion of the N-terminus domain of SUSD4 did not affect NEDD4 binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Mutation of the LPxY site or of both sites completely prevented the binding to NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Furthermore, while the mutation of the PPxY site in the intracellular tail (SUSD4-ΔPY mutant) abrogated binding of NEDD4 only partially, mutation of the LPxY site (SUSD4-ΔLY mutant) or of both sites (SUSD4-ΔPY/LY mutant) completely prevented the binding to NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The extracellular domain of SUSD4 is sufficient for GluA2 interaction.
source: Strong co-immunoprecipitation of GluA2 was detected in anti-HA affinity-purified extracts from cells expressing the HA-tagged extracellular domain of SUSD4 alone (HA-SUSD4-NT construct), showing that this domain is sufficient for GluA2 interaction (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Binding of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases does not affect SUSD4's ability to interact with GluA2.
source: Finally using the SUSD4-ΔLY mutant or SUSD4-ΔPY/LY mutant as a bait did not significantly modify the levels of co-immunoprecipitated GluA2 compared to HA-SUSD4, showing that binding of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases does not affect SUSD4's ability to interact with GluA2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: SUSD4 directly interacts with E3 ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family.
source: We showed that SUSD4 directly interacts with E3 ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family, which are known to regulate ubiquitination and degradation of their substrates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: SUSD4 and GluA2 can interact in transfected HEK293 cells.
source: Our results also show that SUSD4 and GluA2 can interact in transfected HEK293 cells and partially colocalize in cultured PCs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: SUSD4 and GluA2 partially colocalize in cultured PCs.
source: Our results also show that SUSD4 and GluA2 can interact in transfected HEK293 cells and partially colocalize in cultured PCs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: SUSD4 has a function in the regulation of GluA2 trafficking and degradation allowing proper synaptic plasticity and learning.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest a function of SUSD4 in the regulation of GluA2 trafficking and degradation allowing proper synaptic plasticity and learning.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The choice between recycling of AMPA receptors to the membrane or targeting to the endolysosomal compartment for degradation is key for the regulation of the number of AMPA receptors at synapses.
source: The choice between recycling of AMPA receptors to the membrane or targeting to the endolysosomal compartment for degradation is key for the regulation of the number of AMPA receptors at synapses, as well as for the direction and degree of activity-dependent synaptic plasticity (Ehlers, 2000; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Ehlers, 2000 and Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Blocking the trafficking of AMPA receptors through recycling endosomes prevents LTP in neurons.
source: Blocking the trafficking of AMPA receptors through recycling endosomes, for example, using a RAB11 mutant, prevents LTP in neurons (Park et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Park et al., 2004.

claim: Blocking the sorting of AMPA receptors to the endolysosomal compartment impairs LTD in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and cerebellar PCs.
source: Conversely, blocking the sorting of AMPA receptors to the endolysosomal compartment, for example, using a RAB7 mutant, impairs LTD in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and cerebellar PCs (Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Fernández-Monreal et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2017.

claim: In cerebellar PCs, LTD depends on the regulation of the total pool of glutamate receptors.
source: Further support for the role of receptor degradation comes from mathematical modeling showing that in cerebellar PCs LTD depends on the regulation of the total pool of glutamate receptors (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: The GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit and its regulation is of particular importance for LTD.
source: The GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit, and its regulation, is of particular importance for LTD (Diering and Huganir, 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Diering and Huganir, 2018.

claim: Phosphorylation in the C-terminal tail of GluA2 and the binding of molecular partners such as PICK1 and GRIP1/2 regulate endocytosis and recycling.
source: Phosphorylation in its C-terminal tail and the binding of molecular partners such as PICK1 and GRIP1/2 are known to regulate endocytosis and recycling (Bassani et al., 2012; Chiu et al., 2017; Fiuza et al., 2017), and mutations in some of the phosphorylation sites lead to impaired LTD (Chung et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations in some of the phosphorylation sites of GluA2 lead to impaired LTD.
source: Phosphorylation in its C-terminal tail and the binding of molecular partners such as PICK1 and GRIP1/2 are known to regulate endocytosis and recycling (Bassani et al., 2012; Chiu et al., 2017; Fiuza et al., 2017), and mutations in some of the phosphorylation sites lead to impaired LTD (Chung et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2003.

claim: Loss-of-function of Susd4 leads both to loss of LTD and loss of activity-dependent degradation of GluA2 subunits.
source: Our study shows that loss-of-function of Susd4 leads both to loss of LTD and loss of activity-dependent degradation of GluA2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Loss-of-function of Susd4 does not affect degradation of GluD2.
source: Loss-of-function of Susd4 does not affect degradation of another postsynaptic receptor, GluD2, showing the specificity of SUSD4 action.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on western blot data.

claim: Loss-of-function of Susd4 facilitates LTP of PF/PC synapses.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function of Susd4 facilitates LTP of PF/PC synapses.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on electrophysiology data.

claim: SUSD4 has a role in the targeting of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors to the degradation compartment during synaptic plasticity.
source: Overall our results suggest a role for SUSD4 in the targeting of GluA2-containing AMPA receptors to the degradation compartment during synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Adaptor proteins such as GRASP1, GRIP1, PICK1, and NSF promote AMPA receptor recycling and LTP.
source: Adaptor proteins, such as GRASP1, GRIP1, PICK1, and NSF, are known to promote AMPA receptor recycling and LTP (Anggono and Huganir, 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Anggono and Huganir, 2012.

claim: SUSD4 directly binds to HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family.
source: Our results show that SUSD4 directly binds to HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The NEDD4 subfamily is characterized by an N-terminal C2 domain, several WW domains, and the catalytic HECT domain.
source: The family of HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases contains 28 enzymes including the NEDD4 subfamily that is characterized by an N-terminal C2 domain, several WW domains, and the catalytic HECT domain (Weber et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Weber et al., 2019.

claim: NEDD4 E3 ligases add K63 ubiquitin chains to their substrate, a modification that promotes sorting to the endolysosomal compartment for degradation.
source: This subgroup of E3 ligases adds K63 ubiquitin chains to their substrate, a modification that promotes sorting to the endolysosomal compartment for degradation (Boase and Kumar, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Boase and Kumar, 2015.

claim: NEDD4 E3 ligases are highly expressed in neurons in the mammalian brain.
source: NEDD4 E3 ligases are highly expressed in neurons in the mammalian brain and have many known substrates with various functions, including ion channels and the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on known expression patterns.

claim: KO mice for the Nedd4-1 gene die during late gestation.
source: Accordingly, KO mice for the Nedd4-1 gene die during late gestation (Kawabe et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Kawabe et al., 2010.

claim: Both GluA1 and GluA2 AMPA receptor subunits are ubiquitinated on lysine residues in their intracellular tails in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Both GluA1 and GluA2 AMPA receptor subunits are ubiquitinated on lysine residues in their intracellular tails in an activity-dependent manner (Lin et al., 2011; Lussier et al., 2011; Schwarz et al., 2010; Widagdo et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutation of lysine residues in GluA1 and GluA2 decreases localization of these subunits in the endolysosomal compartment in neurons.
source: Mutation of these lysine residues decreases localization of GluA1 and GluA2 AMPA receptor subunits in the endolysosomal compartment in neurons (Widagdo et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Widagdo et al., 2015.

claim: GluA1 and GluA2 subunits lack any obvious intracellular direct binding motif to the WW domain of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases.
source: However, GluA1 and GluA2 subunits lack any obvious intracellular direct binding motif to the WW domain of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases, raising questions about the precise mechanism allowing regulation of AMPA subunits trafficking and degradation by these enzymes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: SUSD4 could regulate the targeting of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases to AMPA receptors in an activity-dependent manner in neurons.
source: SUSD4 could thus regulate the targeting of NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases to AMPA receptors in an activity-dependent manner in neurons.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is a speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: The interaction of SUSD4 with NEDD4 ubiquitin ligases might regulate the trafficking of the SUSD4/GluA2 complex to the degradation pathway.
